articles.title_zh: 数字化之门为东南亚岛民打开福音之门
articles.content: Just as young people today have become more comfortable with talking online than in person, the same is true for people in Southeast Asia. IMB missionaries are creating and publishing Jesus-focused ads, videos and other digital content to connect with the lost through the internet. IMB Photo Recently, an International Mission Board team in Southeast Asia asked a young woman if she had heard the story of Jesus. She replied that, yes, she had heard about Him through a video online! “Back in the day,” shared Amanda Clarkston, an IMB missionary who has served in Southeast Asia for 33 years, “when I first came on the field, you’d go somewhere and gather all the people together in the village to watch the JESUS film.” Now, face-to-face conversations about Christ on the Southeast Asian islands are harder to accomplish. While teams travel to these remote islands often, living in a sparsely populated, animistic background culture as a foreigner creates suspicion and make long-term ministry difficult. Furthermore, young people today have become more comfortable with talking online than they are in person, Clarkston said, which is true of the islanders as well. Attempting to have a spiritual conversation face-to-face has become “too much” for locals, Clarkston shared. So, how do you share the gospel with multiple people groups who are constantly online and less comfortable with in-person interactions? For these Southeast Asia teams, digital engagement — the use of social media platforms to share a message — has become a plausible and effective entry point. The social media agency We Are Social confirmed this, revealing that 82.4% of Southeast Asia’s population uses the internet. “No matter where they go, how far they go, how remote it is, people have phones,” Clarkston and her team realized, “And though sometimes they do have to climb up the highest peak to get reception, people do it.” Clarkston’s team has begun creating and publishing Jesus-focused ads, videos and other digital content in hopes of building bridges to the islanders through the internet. Viewers can click on the ad to message back and forth with a responder, a local believer or missionary who is available to pray, build relationships and answer spiritual questions. “It seems like locals are more open to watching those things in the privacy of their own cell phones,” Clarkston said. Clarkston intends to use digital engagement as a means for initial contact with people with animistic backgrounds, evangelism and, eventually, discipleship. She said that this new ministry has the potential to open doors with individuals across these islands who would normally never reach out on their own or respond to the gospel in person. “Maybe they’ll respond this way,” Clarkston said, “I know without a shadow of a doubt that God is calling people to Himself.” Now, more than ever, technology has a grip on society. Many spend hours each day mindlessly scrolling, searching for meaning, for happiness. And now, more than ever, there is an incredible opportunity to plant seeds across Southeast Asian islands through digital engagement. The IMB Southeast Asia team gives praise to the Lord that He has provided a creative way to reach the lost and plant seeds. Pray the people among the Southeast Asian islands would see these ads and engage with responders boldly, even though they may face persecution or harm because of it. Names were changed for security. articles.content: Ask most people what comes to mind when they think of South Korea, and they’ll likely mention K-pop, skincare, cutting-edge technology, or bustling city streets filled with young professionals. Hun and Eunjoo Sol see those things too. But after more than a decade serving as International Mission Board missionaries in Seoul, they also see something many visitors never notice. “Many people think that Korea is exciting and successful,” Hun said. “They think about the K-pop, the K-culture, K-technology, K-cosmetics. Yes, good things… But many Korean people are struggling right now.” The Sols, who were featured in the 2025 Week of Prayer for International Missions , continue to rely on the prayers of faithful Southern Baptists. Prayers sustain them and help to push back the darkness they confront in their home culture. Hun often describes that hidden struggle with a Korean word: han. There is no simple English translation. It speaks to a deep sorrow shaped by generations of war, division, loss, and the quiet resolve to endure. Hun sees it in the young adults he meets every week—people navigating loneliness and relentless expectations, quietly asking what their lives are for beneath a veneer of success. Han is heavy. For many young adults, that weight can feel unbearable. Suicide is one of the leading causes of death among teenagers and young adults in South Korean. Hun and Eunjoo see the effects of that reality every day, and it’s one reason they believe they have no time to waste. That understanding shaped the week of Serve Tour Seoul this summer. There were no construction sites, no paintbrushes, no tools or work gloves. Instead, the team stepped into ministries local churches had been faithfully building long before the volunteers arrived. In May, 27 volunteers from seven churches across the United States came alongside local churches already serving their communities in Seoul, Paju, and Gwangju. They taught English classes, ran children’s camps, walked neighborhoods in prayer, distributed food, and sat down with college students, one conversation at a time. For Nick Holst of Sandals Church in Riverside, California, the goal was simple enough to say in a sentence: “We came to meet people,” Holst said. “We want to hear their stories, and that leads to some very meaningful connections as you get past the surface into something deeper.” That’s where the week actually lived: past the surface and past the small talk, where the quiet weight of han is often carried without words. On college campuses, volunteers played games, asked questions and mostly just listened. Some conversations lasted a few minutes and ended there. Others kept going long past the point where either person expected them to. One morning, after asking his church back home to pray, Holst sat down with a university student named Intec. They talked about culture first, the way strangers do, and then the conversation turned somewhere neither of them planned. “I got to ask him, ‘What do Koreans believe?’” Holst recalled. Intec said he didn’t believe in God. Then he recited John 3:16 from memory, word for word, a verse he’d heard somewhere along the way and never forgotten. Before they parted, Holst asked if he could pray that God would keep drawing Intec toward Himself. “He said yes.” In a city where many conversations never move beyond the surface, the exchange was a reminder of why the team had come. Not to win an argument, but to listen, to ask questions, and to trust God with what happens next. The same pattern unfolded elsewhere, beginning in classrooms and ending on city streets. Jeremy Doyle, missions pastor at Valley Baptist Church in Bakersfield, California, watched an English conversation club grow from two students on its first night to eight by the second. Nobody advertised it as anything more than a place to practice English, but the room kept filling, and so did the conversations. The team’s work with students didn’t stop there. articles.content: Don Barger, left, IMB director of innovation and artificial intelligence, receives the Excelerate Award at the Missio Nexus Mission Leaders Conference in Orlando, Florida. The award recognizes individuals who demonstrate exceptional leadership and creativity in advancing missions through innovation. Photo provided Don Barger, director of innovation and artificial intelligence for the International Mission Board, received the 2026 Excelerate Award from Missio Nexus during the Mission Leaders Conference, Sept. 24 in Orlando, Florida. According to Missio Nexus, a network of mission-focused organizations and churches, the Excelerate Award recognizes individuals who demonstrate exceptional leadership and creativity in advancing missions through innovation. Barger has earned a reputation for identifying emerging technologies and applying them to ministry challenges, helping pioneer the use of artificial intelligence in global missions while promoting a biblically grounded approach to innovation. Barger said receiving the award was both surprising and encouraging. “I realized it was an affirmation not only of my work, but of the work our entire team has been doing,” he said. “It’s encouraging to see the IMB recognized as an organization willing to invest in innovation, think creatively and explore new ways to reach the nations.” Barger has served with the IMB for 29 years in a variety of roles. He was involved in church planting and led indigenous work in Mexico and Central America. Most of his work as a missionary focused on oral learners and Bible storying. Long before artificial intelligence became mainstream, Barger and his team began examining its potential for missions. IMB team members developed a framework to guide appropriate and inappropriate uses of AI in ministry settings. One principle that continues to shape that framework is Barger’s conviction that “souls should care for souls.” “We do not use AI for counseling or to replace human spiritual care,” Barger said. “Instead, we use AI to handle tasks that free people to spend more time ministering directly to people.” While much of his work centers on technology, Barger emphasizes that innovation extends far beyond technical advances. He defines innovation as a willingness to ask new questions and explore new approaches while remaining faithful to biblical truth. “Too often the response is, ‘That’s not how we’ve always done it,'” Barger said. “Innovation that advances the Great Commission begins by asking new questions and exploring new possibilities.” Barger noted that Christians have a long history of embracing new tools to support gospel ministry, from the printing press to broadcasting and healthcare advances. As artificial intelligence continues to generate discussion among ministry leaders, Barger encourages both optimism and discernment. He points to AI’s potential to improve communication, accelerate training and remove barriers that can hinder ministry efforts. At the same time, he cautions leaders to recognize the limitations of AI and ensure people remain responsible for ministry decisions and engagement. “Every tool throughout history has been capable of both good and evil,” Barger said. “The opportunity is to use AI for redemptive purposes.” Barger’s work includes developing faithbot.tools , a collection of AI tools designed for evangelical Christians. Throughout his career, he has advocated using technology not as an end in itself, but as a means of strengthening ministry and supporting relationships. Looking ahead, Barger hopes his greatest contribution will be encouraging future mission leaders to think creatively while remaining committed to God’s mission. “I hope mission leaders develop a mindset of curiosity,” he said. “Instead of simply accepting, ‘This is how we’ve always done it,’ I want them to ask, ‘How might we do this better?'” For Barger, innovation is ultimately about stewarding available tools in ways that help advance the Great Commission. articles.content: God’s Word transforms lives, strengthens churches and brings hope across generations. Bible translation is part of that story, as communities around the world encounter God’s Word in their own languages. Its future calls for leaders who listen deeply, build trust across cultures and empower others. Within this context, the Wycliffe Global Alliance is searching for its next Executive Director. Could this be your next calling? The Wycliffe Global Alliance is seeking its next Executive Director to serve a worldwide community of more than 100 organisations united in God’s mission through Bible translation. Th e opportunity : Bring our global community together around a shared vision, strengthen local leadership and help a diverse global movement respond to new opportunities with faith and wisdom. The challenge : Lead through change. Articulate a compelling shared vision, strengthen the support the Alliance offers its organisations, and engage support organisations and financial partners in advancing the work. This calls for leadership that honours local autonomy while strengthening global unity, trust, mutual accountability and financial sustainability. We are looking for a leader who brings: A deep commitment to Jesus Christ and a humble, prayerful approach to leadership. At least five years of senior leadership experience and a relevant master’s degree. Proven ability to lead across cultures, develop leaders and empower local churches. Strategic vision, significant fundraising experience and the ability to turn plans into meaningful outcomes. Emotional maturity, integrity and resilience through change. articles.content: Communication staff at 18 Bible translation organizations across Africa need professional training to tell God’s stories well. In November 2026, a one-week workshop in Ruiru, Kenya will teach practical skills like writing, photography, design and video. Then, six months of follow-up support will continue to strengthen networks and create a collaborative culture of sharing God’s stories widely and effectively. Project Name: Africa Area Communication Capacity Building Workshop Implementing Organization: Wycliffe Global Alliance – Africa Area Contact: Phil Prior Director for Communication Wycliffe Global Alliance phil_prior@wycliffe.net Matthew Bore Project Funding Manager Wycliffe Global Alliance matthew_bore@wycliffe.net Start date: September 2026 End date: March 2027 Summary Across Africa, God is moving. Communities are receiving the Bible in their own language for the first time. Lives are being transformed. But too often, these stories never become known beyond the place where they happen. Why? Because not enough people are trained to recognise and report these stories to a wider audience. Among 18 Bible translation organisations across Africa, communication staff are doing their best—but without formal training in news writing, interviewing, photography, video and social media. Many also work in relative isolation without the chance to exchange ideas and collaborate on stories. The result: Amazing stories remain untold, and the people who could be praying, giving or getting involved never learn about the opportunities. This project changes that. For one week (2-6 November 2026) in Ruiru, Kenya, communication staff from those 18 Wycliffe Global Alliance organisations will come together — not just to sit in a classroom, but to actually create. Using smartphones and free tools, they will learn to capture the moments that matter: local communities and churches collaborating; a translation team’s challenges and creative solutions, groups engaging with Scripture, lives being transformed. Attendees also will build plans for how their organisations will keep telling these types of stories long after the workshop ends. Then, over the ensuing six months, this same group will keep coaching, encouraging, and learning from each other — turning 18 separate voices into one strong, unified story of what God is doing across Africa. articles.content: A three-year training program will prepare local translators across Southeast Asia to put the Bible into spoken forms—like storytelling and song—for communities that share knowledge by voice, not writing. Three workshops will build translators’ skills from basic to advanced to mentoring, so at least 20 participants gain local expertise. Project Name: Training Oral Translators Across Southeast Asia Implementing Organization: Wycliffe Global Alliance Contact: Evelyn Gan Consultant for Oral Translation Programmes Wycliffe Global Alliance evelyn_gan@wycliffe.net Start date: FY 2026 End date: FY 2028 Summary Across Southeast Asia, many communities pass along their culture through spoken word—storytelling, song, and drama—rather than through reading and writing. For them, hearing the Bible in these natural forms often connects more deeply than a printed text. Oral Bible Translation is expanding rapidly in Southeast Asia, but the region lacks enough trained people to sustain it. Seminary graduates know the Bible but not oral translation. Practitioners already working need a path to advance their skills. And almost no one is ready to step into consultant roles. Without urgent, structured training, this shortage could stall Oral Bible Translation projects across the region. This three-year project will trains local translators and seminary students in oral Bible translation. Participants move through three stages: a foundation workshop, an advanced workshop and consultant-level training, with only those who show strong skills advancing to the next stage. Our goal is for at least 20 participants, with a smaller group becoming fully qualified to guide future translation projects. Half of the trainers will themselves be new, gaining experience so the program can continue and grow after this project ends. By working in collaboration with Wycliffe Thai Foundation, Wycliffe Malaysia, YWAM Chiang Mai, FCBH, Spoken Worldwide and CRU, the project is rooted in strong partnerships that will ensure sustainability and local ownership. articles.content: Indonesia has hundreds of languages still without Scripture in natural, spoken forms. This three-year program will train 20 local translators and seminary students to fill that gap, building skills from basic to advanced to mentoring. Working with local partners, it aims to grow into a lasting, homegrown training network. Project Name: Training Oral Translators in Indonesia Implementing Organization: Wycliffe Global Alliance Evelyn Gan Consultant for Oral Translation Programmes Wycliffe Global Alliance evelyn_gan@wycliffe.net Start date: FY 2026 End date: FY 2028 Summary Indonesia is home to hundreds of languages whose speakers pass on knowledge through spoken word rather than writing. Most still lack the Bible in a form that feels natural to hear. Oral Bible Translation is expanding quickly in Indonesia, but training hasn’t kept up—seminary graduates lack oral translation skills, and working practitioners have no path to grow or reach consultant-level readiness. Without urgent, structured training, projects across the country risk stalling. This three-year project trains local translators and seminary students to close that gap. Participants move through three stages—foundational, advanced and consultant-level training—with those who show strong skills advancing to the next stage. Our goal is for at least 20 participants, with a smaller group becoming fully qualified to guide future translation projects on their own. The project partners with several Indonesian organizations, including seminaries, so that this training becomes part of local theological education rather than a one-time effort. articles.title: Bible translation’s future is diverse … and local
articles.summary: The ultimate metric of success is no longer just the distribution of physical books, but measurable transformation of lives through deep, culturally authentic understanding.
articles.summary_zh: 衡量成功的最终标准不再仅仅是实体书籍的分发，而是通过深刻的文化真实理解对生活进行可衡量的转变。
articles.title_zh: 圣经翻译的未来是多元化的……和本地
articles.content: Yaoundé, Cameroon — The landscape of global Bible translation is undergoing a paradigm shift, moving away from traditional, agency-led book printing and toward multimodal translations driven by local communities. At a June 2026 gathering in Yaoundé, translation partners and members of Wycliffe Global Alliance organisations spanning Africa, Europe and Latin America reflected on how Scripture is delivered in the 21st century. Their consensus: The ultimate metric of success is no longer just the distribution of physical books, but measurable transformation of lives through deep, culturally authentic understanding. Community-led translation Dr. Paul Kimbi, the Alliance’s Consultant for Bible Translation Programmes, said Bible translation’s future belongs to community dialogue rather than isolated translation agencies. This emerging approach, known as conversational translation, prioritises localised, grassroots work: listening intimately to communities, engaging them in active storytelling and using locally adapted communication channels. As multiple translation agencies increasingly operate within the same borders, global leaders are urging a shift toward radical collaboration. ‘The multiplicity of agencies is not a hindrance; however, harmony and unity are essential,’ Kimbi said. ‘Unity does not mean uniformity. Each agency, according to its unique strengths, approaches Bible translation as a collaborative piece of God’s global mission.’ Multimodal translations will better serve people from different contexts . Beyond the Book: Multimodal and AI Integration Because cultural contexts vary wildly across the globe, the Alliance’s Africa Area gathering highlighted the urgent need for ‘embodied and multimodal’ translations. This means managing multiple streams of communication simultaneously—integrating oral storytelling, vibrant illustrations, written text and digital media. ‘We do not communicate only with words; we communicate with colours, images, and multimedia,’ Kimbi said. ‘We can no longer consider translation strictly as a written book, but rather as a dynamic multimodal experience.’ This digital evolution naturally intersects with the rise of artificial intelligence. While delegates recognised AI’s immense potential to increase translation speed, optimise efficiency and lower operational costs for minority languages, attendees maintained a stance of strategic caution. ‘Technology accelerates the advancement of Bible translation and language development, but it also creates new strategic responsibilities for leaders and organisations,’ said Etienne Ondoa, a language technology consultant. Staff capacity building, therefore, remains the greatest investment, he said. As technology evolves, the skills required to support it in ministry also evolve. ‘Technological leadership should have a voice in strategic decision-making processes, Ondoa said. ‘Technological decisions increasingly influence ministry outcomes, sound financial resource management, cybersecurity, AI adoption and organisational resilience.’ Etienne Ondoa A Symphony for the Global Church Ultimately, leaders at the event reaffirmed that translation organisations do not operate in a vacuum. They exist to serve the church, which remains God’s primary vehicle for global mission. Kimbi likened the future of the movement to a grand, global arrangement. ‘The particularity of modern Bible translation is that it is a diverse ensemble—an orchestra of varied influences interpreting a magnificent symphony titled ‘Scriptures’ for every language community,’ he said. ‘And in this orchestra, we need everyone: local churches, oral communicators, media creators, literacy specialists and technology partners.’ Story: Lune Prudence Mvondo and Isaac Forchie Photos: Isaac Forchie
articles.content_zh: 喀麦隆雅温得 全球圣经翻译的地貌正在发生范式转变,从传统的、机构主导的书籍印刷转向由当地社区驱动的多模式翻译。 在2026年6月的雅温得集会上,翻译伙伴和遍布非洲、欧洲和拉丁美洲的维克利夫全球联盟组织的成员反思了21世纪如何交付《圣经》。 他们的共识: 衡量成功与否的终极尺度不再仅仅是物理图书的发行,而是通过深刻,文化上真实的理解,对生活进行可测量的转变. 联盟的圣经翻译方案顾问Paul Kimbi博士说,圣经翻译的未来属于社区对话而不是孤立的翻译机构。 这种新兴方法被称为对话翻译、地方化优先化、基层工作:密切听取社区的意见,让他们参与积极讲故事,并使用适合当地情况的交流渠道。 随着多个翻译机构越来越多地在同一边界内运作,全球领导人正在敦促向根本合作转变。 Kimbi说 : “ 机构繁多并非障碍, `团结并不意味着统一。 每个机构都根据其独特的长处,将圣经翻译视为上帝全球使命的合作作品。 多式联运将更好地为来自不同背景的人服务。 除了《书:多式联运和人工智能一体化》之外,由于世界各地的文化背景大相径庭,联盟的非洲地区会议强调迫切需要 " 健全和多模式 " 翻译。 这意味着同时管理多种通信流——将口头讲故事、活泼的插图、书面文字和数字媒体结合起来。 Kimbi说 : “ 我们不只用文字沟通, 我们不能再严格地认为翻译是一本书, 这种数字演变自然地与人工智能的兴起相交. 虽然代表们承认大赦国际在提高翻译速度、优化效率和降低少数民族语言的业务费用方面具有巨大潜力,但与会者保持战略谨慎的立场。 语言技术顾问Etienne Ondoa说, “技术加速了圣经翻译和语言发展的进步, 因此,他说,工作人员的能力建设仍然是最大的投资。 随着技术的发展,部内支持技术所需的技能也随之而来. Ondoa说,“技术领导在战略决策进程中应有发言权。 “技术决定日益影响部委的成果、健全的财政资源管理、网络安全、人工智能的采用和组织复原力。” Etienne Ondoa是全球教会的交响乐团, 它们的存在是为了为教会服务,而教会仍然是上帝执行全球任务的主要工具。 金比把运动的未来比作一个宏伟的全球安排. 他说,“现代圣经译本的特殊性在于它是一个多样化的合唱团——由各种影响组成的管弦乐团,为每个语言群体解释一首名为 " 脚本 " 的宏伟交响乐。 “在这个管弦乐团中,我们需要每个人:地方教会、口头宣传者、媒体创造者、扫盲专家和技术伙伴。” 故事:吕恩·普鲁登斯·姆冯多和艾萨克·福奇相片:艾萨克·福奇相片

articles.title: God’s mission in Africa: ‘There is still much to do’
articles.summary: For both the African and global audiences at the Yaoundé gathering, panel members underscored a fundamental truth: Bible translation is not an isolated academic exercise.
articles.summary_zh: 在雅温得会议上，小组成员向非洲和全球观众强调了一个基本事实：圣经翻译并不是一项孤立的学术活动。
articles.title_zh: 神在非洲的使命： “还有很多事情要做”
articles.content: YAOUNDÉ, CAMEROON — During the Wycliffe Global Alliance Africa Area Gathering, a question was put before delegates: Is the African Church awake? A three-person panel, moderated by Dr. Zac Manyim, Director of the Department of Church and Scripture Engagement at CABTAL (Cameroon Association for Bible Translation and Literacy), delved into the continent’s strategic mission challenges and local breakthroughs. A Call from the Pulpit to Action ‘Yes, the African Church is awake, but it is not active,’ said Rev. Abel Chebe Ngah of the Apostolic Church in Cameroon. He noted a disparity in how modern ministry resources are being spent. ‘Some churches are focused on building megachurches, while only a few are focused on spreading the Word of God. The African church should have been doing exploits, but it is not yet doing so. There are still many areas in Africa not reached by the gospel.’ For the landscape to shift, Ngah argued that mission cannot be treated lightly; the local church must intentionally send missionaries. Demonstrating local ownership, his own denomination dedicates a specific Sunday every year entirely to Bible translation, using it to mobilise believers and raise financial support for CABTAL’s fieldwork. Though some local churches might lack the required financial resources, they offer abundant human and material resources needed in Bible translation. The Lifelong Impact of Mother-Tongue Literacy Pastor Alphonse Gamaldak, president of the Mofu Gudur Inter-Church Committee, said Bible translation reshaped his entire life trajectory. Before receiving any formal education, he learned to read and write in his mother tongue. This linguistic foundation gave him the leeway to master French, eventually leading him to seminary. ‘Yes, the church is awake in Mofu Gudur (a language community of northern Cameroon) because many kids have now grown and seen their lives transformed by the Bible translated into our language,’ he said. The impact extends far beyond the sanctuary. Through mother-tongue functional literacy programmes overseen by the translation project, community members have developed income-generating activities, drastically improving local livelihoods. Today, over 250 literacy teachers are actively instructing inside churches and surrounding villages. Yet, Pastor Gamaldak warned that sustainability requires ongoing investment. ‘There is still much to do,’ he said, ‘like continuing to build the capacity of and support these 250 literacy teachers.’ In 2008, when the Mofu Gudur New Testament was dedicated, the church and the community came together to facilitate the distribution. Five thousand copies were printed, and they were all sold out in the following months. A second run of 4,000 copies was printed. A few years later, it was still hard to obtain a copy. This motivated CABTAL to begin work on the Old Testament, which was dedicated in May 2026. Thanks to the commitment of the local church, the Mofu Gudur people now have a complete Bible. The Takeaway for the Global Alliance For both the African and global audiences at the Yaoundé gathering, panel members underscored a fundamental truth: Bible translation is not an isolated academic exercise. When local churches move from being merely ‘awake’ to being actively engaged, Scripture access unlocks deep spiritual maturity, local resource mobilisation and holistic community development. Story and Photos: Isaac Forchie
articles.content_zh: 在威克里夫全球联盟非洲地区集会期间,向代表们提出了一个问题: 非洲教会醒了吗? 一个三人小组,由CABTAL(喀麦隆圣经翻译和识字协会)教会和圣经参与部主任Zac Manyim博士主持,探讨了非洲大陆的战略任务挑战和地方突破。 喀麦隆使徒教会的Abel Chebe Ngah牧师说, 他指出,在现代部委资源如何使用方面存在差距。 :"有些教堂专注于建造特大教堂,而只有少数教堂专注于传播"上帝之道". 非洲教会本应在进行剥削,但尚未这样做。 非洲仍有许多地区没有获得福音。 为了改变地貌,Ngarh认为不能轻视任务;当地教会必须故意派遣传教士. 他自己的教派每年专门用一个礼拜天翻译圣经, 尽管一些地方教会可能缺乏所需的财政资源,但它们提供了圣经翻译所需的大量人力和物力资源。 Mofu Gudur教会间委员会主席Alphonse Gamaldak教授的《母亲-通格识字牧师终身影响》说,《圣经》翻译重塑了他的整个人生轨迹。 在接受任何正规教育之前,他学会用母语读写. 这个语言学基础给了他掌握法语的回旋余地,最终引导他进入神学院. 他说 : “ 是的, 教堂在Mofu Gudur(喀麦隆北部的一个语言社区)醒了, 因为许多孩子已经长大, 影响远远超出避难所。 通过翻译项目监督的母语实用识字方案,社区成员开展了创收活动,大大改善了当地生计。 今天,250多名扫盲教师正在教会内部和周围的村庄积极进行教学。 然而,Gamaldak牧师警告说,可持续性需要持续投资。 他说,“还有许多事情要做,就像继续建设和支持这250名扫盲教师的能力。” 2008年,当"莫福古都尔新约"被奉献时,教会与社区聚集一堂来为发行提供便利. 印出五千本,后数月全部被卖出. 第二次印制了4000册. 几年后,仍难以获得副本. 这激励了CABTAL开始"旧约"的工作,该"旧约"于2026年5月被专门化. 由于当地教会的承诺,莫福古都尔人现在有了完整的"圣经". 小组成员强调了一个基本真理:圣经翻译不是孤立的学术活动。 当当地教会从仅仅是`觉醒'走向积极参与时,《圣经》的获取将释放出深刻的精神成熟、地方资源动员和整体社区发展。 故事与相片:以撒·福奇
